#203. Trump’s shattered ‘mirror world’: American voters roundly reject president’s alternate reality

President claimed to have ushered in a ‘golden age’ even as prices soared and war dragged on – and midterm voters did not buy his looking-glass narrative

A new “golden age of America” is under way, Donald Trump repeatedly declared in his final pitch to voters before the US midterm elections.

The war in Iran was not really a war, because “we’ve done very little fighting”, the US president stressed. The stock market had hit 88 all-time highs. “They’re saying,” he said, that on his watch the US has become “the hottest country anywhere in the world”.

“We’ve achieved more in less than two years than any administration in American history, and I’ve kept every single promise I made – except far more,” he claimed in an extraordinary speech at Washington’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool on the last day of the campaign. “I’ve actually kept far more promises than I made. We’ve done much more than I promised.”

As Americans prepared to cast their vote in hundreds of congressional races across the country, Trump implored them to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, and vote on the policies he had enacted.

This “mirror world” – Trump’s constructed reality, casting his enemies as democracy-stealing villains and himself as the savior – was a central pillar of his victorious bid to reclaim the White House two years ago. As votes were counted on Tuesday night, though, it became clear the mirror had shattered.

Americans, including those who went for Trump in the past, weren’t buying his narrative. They didn’t approve of the Iran war, and weren’t experiencing a “golden age” as they filled up their cars and paid for groceries.

Across the US, however, the Guardian spoke to voters who made clear they accepted one element of Trump’s alternate reality as they entered polling places: they did consider his administration, and agenda, to be on the ballot – much to the devastation of Republicans running for office up and down the ballot.

“One by one,” said Tom Galvin, a Republican on the Maricopa county board of supervisors in Arizona, “everything that was important” to the coalition of voters that carried him back to power in 2024 fell by the wayside.

“For example, if you wanted the Epstein files, that didn’t happen,” said Galvin. “If you wanted to address inflation because Biden had runaway inflation, well, that didn’t happen. If you wanted to see a relief in gas prices, that didn’t happen. If you didn’t want us to get into‘foreign wars or senseless wars’, that didn’t happen.”

Later in the week, Trump remained defiant about his role in his party’s collapse. He elevated Stephen Miller, one of the most controversial figures in his administration, to chief of staff.

“I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT,” he wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE!”

Voters in Tuesday’s election explained the economy – particularly their inability to afford their lives – was central to their decisions. But corruption under Trump, the Iran war, tariffs, datacenters, healthcare costs and the administration’s aggressive deportation scheme weighed into their votes.

“There’s a war that nobody wants right now,” Jim Conrad, a voter in Ohio, told the Guardian. Ron Miller, in Kansas, said he was for Trump, but acknowledged that the president “hasn’t done anything” to lower the cost of living. Todd Cox, in Maine, cited “the disregard for the rule of law”, while Linda Olson, in Kansas, a previous Trump voter, said the president was now working to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”.

Voters who usually split their tickets between the two parties’ candidates said they wanted to send a message. As Stacey, a voter in Iowa, told the Guardian: “I wanted to vote for no Republicans.”

Rather than acknowledge voters’ woes, Trump tried for months to explain, or dismiss, them. Affordability, he said last year, was a “con job” perpetrated by Democrats. Fuel prices may be high for consumers, but “the United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars”, he said in October. People who don’t want datacenters in their communities will end up “backwards and poor”, he said this summer. He was “willing to do tariffs” and they have helped US companies, he said in Kansas just before the election.

“You don’t see the stock market on the side of the road. But you drive down a street, you see the gas prices,” said Paul Bentz, an independent pollster and strategist at HighGround, an Arizona public affairs firm. “The tone-deaf nature of his approach on things, talking about issues that other folks don’t care about, ignoring and pretending like there aren’t struggles going on, just was not the right strategy.”

Bentz’s colleague described it as the reflecting pool election. Trump delivered his final speech before an algae-beset pool of water he spent 14m renovating that showed him his own reflection: “Narcissism 101”, a metaphor for the midterms.

Jim Abeler, a Republican state senator in Minnesota who lost his reelection bid this month, knocked on the doors of about 80% of the homes in his district. He encountered a lot of “outright hostility” toward Trump over gas prices and the Iran war, and some voters refused to talk to him because of it.

He didn’t hear voters saying that Trump’s rhetoric or his attempts to explain away economic concerns were the problem; it was the economics themselves. Half of the people he talked to were “unforgiving”, he said.

One woman who said she usually voted for Democrats but also had voted for Abeler in previous elections said she couldn’t do it this year. “She said, ‘I’m sorry, it’s just a bad year to be you,’” he recalled.

Chris Madel, a Minneapolis attorney who was running in the Republican primary for Minnesota governor until he dropped out and criticized his party over the deportation onslaught into the state, said he knew in January – amid the Operation Metro Surge crackdown – that this would end poorly for Republicans.

“The people that were showing that fealty towards him and towards this one person,” Madel said. “The tone deafness was really without equal.”

Madel said he asked his Trump-supporting family members whether they “think it’s OK” for the US president to accept “a 747 for free” from Qatar, for example. The attorney never thought the US would look like “a banana republic with respect to corruption”, he added.

Democratic candidates said for months that voters, including those in red-leaning areas, just wanted to feel heard. They centered their campaigns around in-person town halls, went to county fairs, and returned to retail politics.

People “don’t feel that the federal government really gives a damn about them”, Rebecca Cooke, a Democrat running for a Republican-held congressional district in western Wisconsin, said just before the election. She won.

Erin Klaus, who owns a small business in Cooke’s district that will close at the end of this year after weathering economic pains the last two years, said it has felt like the message from the government was that her problems weren’t really happening.

“The federal government can say that the prices are going down, and inflation is going down. But, I mean, that’s just not true in our daily lives,” she told the Guardian in October. “I think it’s really hard to continue to be told these things that we know aren’t true and feel almost like we’re getting mocked for the hardships that we’re enduring – both as business owners and as just regular folks, trying to live their lives.”

Bob Brooks, a Democrat who flipped Pennsylvania’s 7th congressional district, said voters were “frustrated with a guy who was promising them one thing” but gave them “something completely different”.

In short, “they felt lied to by the Trump organization, anybody that supported him, and they’re looking for change”, he added. “The status quo is not OK.”

After epic losses, Republican party leaders are searching for what comes next – and considering how tied their futures are to Trump.

Galvin, the Maricopa county supervisor, said the people in his party who either stayed home, or voted the other way, were trying to send a message: stop excusing corruption and trafficking in election lies, and get to work on real issues that matter to voters.

Republicans didn’t seriously attempt to distance themselves from Trump. Breaking with him would have been a major political risk in the Republican primaries, where the party faithful remained supportive of Trump. But by the time polls closed on 3 November, Arizona Republicans lost handily up and down the ballot - both chambers of the state legislature flipped, and the Democratic governor won her reelection bid by nearly 13 points – a stomping victory in a battleground state.

But “there is a lane to do the right thing” in the Republican party, according to Galvin. He had argued that tariffs were wrong. He heard from voters concerned about corruption in Washington after seeing what looked like pay-to-play pardon schemes. “I didn’t see any federal officials in Arizona, or federal candidates in Arizona on our side, say anything about that,” he said.

“Federal candidates in Arizona did not fully convey that they appreciate people’s pain,” he said. “I think they they whistled past the graveyard.”

Joe Pitts, a Republican who leads Arizona think tank 1912 Institute, said he’s not ready to count out Trump, or his influence in the party. A lot of the quick conclusions offered this week will look wrong in a few months, he suggested. “So long as Trump is president and frankly, so long as Trump is alive, he will exercise significant influence over the Republican Party.”

Pitts also warned that the significant shifts do not signal broad approval for Democrats, but that these demographics are all up for grabs and willing to change their minds. The massive losses could, in time, mean there opportunities for Republicans, he said.

Abeler, the Minnesota state senator who lost his race, predicted that the presidential election could go better for Republicans because people got protest votes off their chests.

Democrats, too, have been careful not to interpret the results as a broad endorsement of their party, but a sign that people are sick of politics as usual – including the way the president talks about the issues that affect them directly.

“People are just tired of nonsense. They’re tired of people performing in front of them,” said Brooks, the Pennsylvania Democrat. “People are tired of the show. I don’t want to be a show. I just want to help people.”

Christine Hunschofsky, a Florida state representative and the incoming House Democratic leader in the state, said in a media call this week that elected officials in both parties should see the election results as a call to listen to voters and address their concerns, or they will be voted out, no matter how safe a seat seems for either party.

People no longer trust that their government will respond to their needs because they keep hearing from candidates who say they care and then not seeing any action when those candidates take office, she said,

“Every elected official has such a responsibility right now to restore that trust,” Hunschofsky said. “Because once that trust is gone, I have even bigger concerns for our country.”

#202. From the front row to the hot seat — what the midterms mean for Big Tech

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Right before the midterm elections, OpenAI hired Jessica Schumer, daughter of Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer. The company also said it would start calling its data centers “compute campuses.”

For the past two years, many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names have built closer ties with President Donald Trump and his administration. Several attended White House events, some companies scaled back diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and some executives donated millions to super PACs supporting his campaign and allied candidates. Administration policies also benefited the industry, including tax breaks, the pausing of some federal investigations, and looser AI regulation. Meanwhile, Meta faced lawsuits and billion-dollar fines, and OpenAI faced suits alleging its technology harmed users.

Now, with the midterms shifting the balance of power in Washington, those same companies are working to rebuild ties with Democrats, who have pledged to tighten oversight of AI. How far that gets them may depend less on image-polishing than on where the real fights are happening: in state capitols, in communities deciding whether to host data centers, and, as we’ve seen this past week, in the markets watching the AI boom.

J.B. Branch, director of federal AI governance and technology policy at Public Citizen, a nonprofit advocacy group that describes itself as nonpartisan, told me that the tech industry “realizes they have an optics problem.” He characterized moves like the Schumer hire and the rebranding as “PR washing.” He expects more of it, too, pointing to OpenAI’s partnership with the American Federation of Teachers, announced last year, as well as Anthropic’s newly launched Claude Corps and Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. “I would imagine more of that sort of investment in these corporate, private-public partnerships,” he said.

These initiatives didn’t spring up overnight. Meta and other tech companies reportedly began looking for ways to strengthen their ties to Democrats as Democratic gains in the midterms looked more likely. Reached for comment about the midterm elections’ impact on Meta, a company spokesperson pointed TechCrunch to remarks that Meta President Dina Powell McCormick made this week at WSJ Tech. “You have to work with the government that the American people elect,” McCormick had said. “I have seen it across the board that you have to be bipartisan, and you want to be, because you want buy-in on the things that you’re trying to do.”

Not everyone expects them to work. Alice Marwick, director of research at the tech policy nonprofit Data & Society, told me she expects Big Tech to try to pivot back toward the middle, “if not the left. But it’s a little too late,” she said. “Tech companies should be asking themselves how their products can make people’s lives better, because right now, it doesn’t seem like they are.”

If Democrats follow through on pledges to tighten oversight of AI and Big Tech, the industry could face a tougher environment. Data center moratoriums are gaining traction, and a wave of AI regulation bills awaits drafting. At the same event, Powell McCormick said Meta wants to show that communities welcoming its investments will see “an enormous amount of benefit,” while those that don’t want them “will of course have the right to stop them.”

Still, the next two years could bring political gridlock in Washington. Aryan Ranjan, founder of Baraza, a political campaign management software company, told me most action will likely happen at the state level, since states have already sued tech companies and passed regulations. “A coalition built on newer, working-class voters is likely to push Democrats to frame AI around electricity bills, data-center siting and jobs rather than abstract AI safety,” he said of what to expect at the federal level.

Last December, the Trump administration signed an executive order creating the AI Litigation Task Force, a federal group meant to challenge state AI laws. The administration has argued that U.S. AI companies “must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulations.” Many states have nonetheless passed their own laws, including measures on chatbots and deepfakes.

It also remains to be seen how President Trump will respond, including whether he’ll sign more AI executive orders or veto bills that could be seen as anti-AI. Clearly, voters want stronger guardrails around the technology.

In a statement to TechCrunch, a White House official said: “American leadership in super intelligence is essential for our national security, economic prosperity, and the quality of life of the American people. President Trump is committed to ensuring America continues to lead the world in super intelligence while protecting American consumers. As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.”

Branch argued that Trump’s political fortunes are now tied to the AI industry. On Wednesday, the day after the midterms, a trillion-dollar market sell-off spooked investors, some are whom are reportedly now reconsidering Anthropic’s reported trillion-dollar IPO. “There’s a very strong likelihood that there will be an AI bubble pop, and it’ll happen on Trump’s hands,” Branch said, predicting a possible market collapse. “Does he want to sink or swim along with the AI industry?”

For now, the rules companies face may vary by location. “For the next two years, a company’s AI rules may depend more on where it operates rather than on anything Washington passes,” Ranjan said.

#201. South Africa's ANC facing worst-ever performance in local elections

Near-final results show South Africa's once dominant ANC will see its lowest-ever vote percentage. The party is taking the blame for shoddy municipal services, including water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) is heading for an historically poor election performance, with the near-final tally from Wednesday's municipal polls showing it coming in with just over 30% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said Saturday in sharing the results after 98% of votes were counted.

South African voters in 2026 are angry about water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities.  High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are other pressing issues.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed the poor performance as of Saturday evening. However, during the week, he admitted in his weekly presidential letter that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

Although the ANC will still be the single largest party by overall vote percentage, it had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

South Africa is now looking at complex coalition negotiations for municipal level governing alliances.

Runner up in the polls looks to be the pro-business, center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), coming in at 24% of the votes.

The DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

#199. Dogecoin jumps after Elon Musk replaces Twitter bird with Shiba Inu

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”

It wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

#197. Sequoia shutting down its Scouts program marks the end of an era

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Sequoia this week announced a broad overhaul in a memo posted to X, a move that includes closing its London office and shutting down its scout program. Observers warn that it would be a mistake to read too much into the London closure, since the British capital has a thriving AI scene. On the other hand, the decision to end scouts says more about where venture investing is headed.

That’s partly because 17 years ago, Sequoia pioneered the scouts model, in which select founders and operators write checks on the firm’s behalf. Amid increased competition for deal flow, many VC firms followed suit. But a consensus now seems to be emerging that the model has reached its limits in its current form.

Not everyone was sold on the model in the first place. “They pioneered the scout program but [to be honest] it never made sense to me!” VC Sheel Mohnot wrote on X this week. “The scouts themselves don’t really care that much about the investments, you can still miss (like they did with Uber), not sure what it gets you. I suspect other firms will shutter theirs too,” he added.

To be clear, Sequoia didn’t make a case against scouts in the memo. Instead, it framed its decision as part of a broader need for more focus. But its goal of “putting more energy behind fewer people and things” is likely to resonate with others who’ve questioned the ‘spray and pray’ approach to scouting.

Rival firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), for instance, rolled out a global scout network aimed at spotting opportunities in the U.S. and also in smaller European hubs. But a16z partner Gabriel Vasquez told TechCrunch earlier this year that the firm had revamped its program to double down “on the best people.”

Under this new approach, Vasquez explained, scouts get more resources but are also expected to be more active, such as by co-hosting dinners with the firm. “They get more budget, but we have reduced the number,” he said.

This also seems to indicate that it is VC firms that have been driving an overhaul of the model. For founders, being a scout is attractive: it brings them closer to firms they may want checks from someday, or even a partner role with, and being seen as someone who can write a check can raise their standing among other founders.

Some scouts will undoubtedly mourn the end of Sequoia’s program. Among them is Station F boss Roxanne Varza, who wrote on LinkedIn that she was “sad” to hear that the program was getting cut off, and “hope[d] that other funds [w]on’t follow suit.”

Varza, a former Sequoia scout from 2020 to 2025, told TechCrunch that she had no information beyond what has been shared publicly, but observed that becoming a scout had often been a stepping stone for aspiring investment managers.

“I cannot name all of the incredible scouts that have gone on to join or build funds, but there are quite a few. And the scout programs may have helped them get there — allowed them to build an investment track record, allowed them to build relationships with various funds directly, and more,” she wrote to TechCrunch.

According to Varza, the program’s impact went beyond the individual level, instead helping the entire ecosystem become more mature. “I believe they have helped to foster the investment culture and early-stage investment landscape that we now see in Europe, for example,” Varza said.

While others may agree with Varza about the role these programs have played, they may still have run their course for two reasons. First, seasoned operators may get more financial upside as angels. When it’s their own money, they get to keep the returns, too. Second, leading VC firms are now big and well-known enough that the best founders tend to come to them, so they worry less about missing deals, except at the very earliest stages or in niches and geographies where they have less reach.

Still, the pull of those early and niche deals is why scouts programs are much more likely to get revamped than to disappear entirely. “While Sequoia may be cutting the program, venture partner-style deals are likely to continue,” said Varza in her email to TechCrunch. “Scouts was just a way to scale the format. I don’t imagine Sequoia would end all forms of venture partners, but they are full of surprises.”

#196. From the overblown to the ordinary? Met Gala 2027 to celebrate ‘poetics of everyday’

Event regarded as Oscars of fashion industry replaces John Galliano retrospective with homage to the ‘extra ordinary’

A few months after the planned John Galliano Met Gala retrospective was cancelled amid a backlash focused on the designer’s past, a more commonplace theme has been announced: “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday.” It has left some commentators speculating that celebrities might replace the couture “omelette dresses” and four-part red-carpet performances with jeans and a nice top.

While the dress code for the next Met Gala, which will be held on 3 May 2027, is yet to be announced, it traditionally derives from the exhibition theme.

According to a press release, extraORDINARY will “explore how designers rework familiar garments, everyday objects, and commonplace materials”. Taking wardrobe staples and everyday materials – “from jeans, T-shirts and puffer coats to paper, plastic and metal” – it will “examine how design reveals unexpected possibilities within everyday things”.

Reactions have been mixed. For Dana Thomas, the author of Gods and Kings: The Rise and Fall of Alexander McQueen and John Galliano, it “reinforces the message that was very, very clear with the Galliano announcement that the costume institute’s team is highly out of touch”. She characterises the decision to “take such ordinary garments and then show how fashion has co-opted them and added zeros to the price tag” as tone deaf.

It is also, she says, a “missed opportunity”. Thomas is among those who think the theme would have been better off honouring some of the biggest names from the worlds of fashion and popular culture who have died this year, including Dolly Parton and Bob Mackie, the designer responsible for the “naked” dress worn by Cher to the Met Gala in 1974 and many of Parton’s costumes over the years. “There could have been a Bob Mackie room in the Dolly Parton show.” It would, she says, “have been easy and it would have been a beautiful homage to a woman who was a style icon and a humanitarian”.

Thomas also thinks it would have “been enormous – it would have made the museum a ton of money, it would have gotten a lot of goodwill from the press. It would have been loved by Americans and tourists in New York alike.” Instead, she says, “fun is missing from the equation”.

According to 1Granary, a platform known for holding the industry to account: “The new Met Gala theme proves that sometimes fashion is either too controversial to exist or too boring to care about.” For Malique Morris, a correspondent at Line Sheet, an industry newsletter, his underwhelm stems from the fact it came “in the wake of a Galliano exhibit”. “Because we’re not getting that, we’re going to feel robbed,” he says.

Others online point out that this new theme feels about as far from the fantastical work of the famed couturier Galliano, who was found guilty of a hate crime in 2011 after a series of racist and antisemitic rants, as it’s possible to get.

But for some commentators, extraORDINARY is cause for celebration and intrigue. According to the celebrity stylist and Vogue contributor Marian Kwei, the theme is “very clever”. It seems, she says, “very simple, but it’s far from it. It’s actually a very interesting thing, which I think is an incredible celebration of fashion, the concept of fashion design and what designers try to do with design itself.”

As for how the theme could translate on to the red carpet: “it could be a palette cleanser,” says Morris, “maybe a bit of a refresh. Instead of the constant peacocking, trying to have a viral moment … there could be a sense of just look good, make sure the clothes fit you well, tell a story and that story doesn’t have to be incredibly high glam.”

There is a red carpet precedent for staples like denim. The American designer Zac Posen, in his capacity as creative director of Gap, has been responsible for lots of these trends, including at the Met. In 2024 Da’vine Joy Randolph wore an all-denim creation by Posen to the gala. At last year’s event, the Australian pop star Troye Sivan wore devoré-effect jeans by Prada and the model Bhavitha Mandava wore muslin-printed trousers made to look like blue jeans by Matthieu Blazy at Chanel.

Perhaps the exhibition’s focus on “recycling, upcycling and reuse” will see the work of designers such as the Swedish designer Ellen Hodakova Larsson, who creates couture gowns out of belt buckles and old spoons, worn to the event. Kwei speculates that the work of the Dutch designer Duran Lantink, who does “incredible things with everyday materials”, may be a good fit.

With individual tickets last year going for about $100,000, there is nothing everyday about the guest list, which is personally overseen by Anna Wintour. There are, says Kwei, opportunities for missteps “when it is attended by people who are not really in touch with the context of the times”. It is, she says, “going to be very interesting for the red carpet”.

#195. Stimulant overdoses on the rise as opioid deaths decline, but treatment is complex

More people recognize opioid overdoses, but education about stimulant overdoses hasn’t been as clear-cut

Overdoses involving stimulants are on the rise in many parts of the country, according to recently available data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but experts say recognizing and responding to them is more complex when compared with opioid overdoses.

“The rate of overdose decline was not nearly what we expected” in California, said Dr Taylor Nichols, an emergency and addiction medicine physician based in Sacramento.

Nichols said that stimulants “filled the gap” left by declining fentanyl overdoses. Methamphetamine and cocaine are the most common illicit stimulants.

While fentanyl-involved overdose deaths dropped to pre-pandemic levels nationally for the first time in 2025, per provisional CDC overdose fatality data, deaths involving cocaine went up in 13 states and deaths involving methamphetamine went up in eight states. In some states, like Arizona, non-fatal stimulant overdoses are reaching record highs.

Public health messaging has been effective at teaching people to recognize opioid overdoses and respond to them with naloxone, but education about stimulant overdoses and how to handle them hasn’t been as clear-cut.

“As a bystander, it is a lot more challenging to decide whether something is a stimulant overdose when you compare to how clear-cut a true opioid overdose is,” said Stephen Murray, director of SafeSpot Overdose Hotline, a safety service for people using drugs alone run out of Boston medical center.

A former paramedic, Murray runs overdose response trainings for paramedics across the country. When someone’s breathing has slowed down dramatically or stopped, it’s a clear sign of opioid overdose, but stimulant overdoses vary widely.

“A stimulant overdose can be as simple as releasing too much stimulation into your brain and into your body,” said Nichols. Extreme overstimulation strains the heart and brain, leading to heart attacks and strokes.

Nichols and Murray both recommend learning how to recognize strokes and other stimulant overdose symptoms. The Be Fast mnemonic (Balance loss, Eyesight changes, Face droop, Arm [or leg] weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911) lays out signs of stroke. Stimulant-induced shortness of breath, seizure and chest pain also warrant immediate medical attention.

Calling 911 is advised for any overdose, but bystanders do successfully save lives using naloxone without involving medical professionals. There are no equivalent tools for bystanders witnessing a stimulant-induced heart attack, stroke or seizure. If someone loses consciousness during a stimulant overdose, it could indicate opioids are involved as well, and it is safe to use naloxone to reverse the possible opioid component.

High doses of stimulants are especially dangerous in hot climates.

“You can develop hyperthermia, where your body gets too hot, and that can end up resulting in significant brain damage or death,” Nichols explained. People using stimulants sometimes forget to eat or drink, but Murray said that a conscious effort to stay hydrated can prevent overheating.

Dalton Barrett, a paramedic and manager of opioid settlement funds in rural Edgecombe county, North Carolina, recommends getting stimulant overdose patients as calm as possible while waiting for an ambulance to arrive. That means getting rid of external stimulation, like music, bright lights and crowds.

“What we don’t want to happen is we get over there, and now they’re aggressive with the EMS staff, and now law enforcement’s coming, and the person gets tased or maced or put in handcuffs,” Barrett said. These kinds of altercations are distressing for patients, and can also make it harder for emergency responders to treat them.

Prolonged, sleepless stimulant binges can also lead to psychosis and paranoia.

“I have a history of meth and stimulant use, and have been in quasi-meth psychosis before,” Murray said. “Telling someone that [their delusion] is not happening doesn’t make it feel less real.” Murray instead suggests validating that the experience is scary. “If you’re preparing for an EMS arrival for someone you love, just make sure that that person isn’t going to be perceived as being threatening,” Murray said. This can mean calmly looking around the space and clearing anything that might appear incriminating, like a weapon.

Ideally, Murray said, emergency medical services and law enforcement coordinate to keep patients safe, especially when they need to be restrained. One way he recommends advocating for patients who are forcibly restrained is to make sure they’re receiving medical sedatives as well.

Most fatal stimulant overdoses also involve other substances, but Murray notes that older men with heart health problems are most at risk of dying from stimulants alone.

“The people who die have the American diet and lack of exercise sort of stuff going on. Then when you mix in high-potency stimulants, especially if people are injecting them, that is a deadly combination,” he said, adding that he wishes that people could talk openly with their doctors about their drug use and health, because broader strategies to improve heart health can also help prevent stimulant overdoses, even when someone continues to use stimulants. Still, drug criminalization and abstinence-only messaging make this difficult.

He continued: “It is really challenging for us to study how we could improve people’s health in this situation, because we just tell people not to use drugs, when we know that millions of people every year in the US spend billions of dollars on stimulants.”

#194. Amazon’s new basic Kindle proves you don’t need all the bells and whistles

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

In October, Amazon announced its refreshed Kindle lineup, its first significant design overhaul in years. The highlights included a new edge-to-edge design that eliminated traditional raised bezels, thinner and lighter Paperwhite and Colorsoft models with better displays, and page-turning accessories like a Bluetooth remote and a magnetic cover with page-turn buttons.

However, given the impact of the global memory-chip shortage driven by the AI boom, the new Kindles also debuted with pricing that had increased by $40 to $50 across the lineup. That makes it more difficult for the average consumer to consider buying one of the more premium devices.

For that reason, the Kindle I most wanted to get my hands on was the 6-inch entry-level device, which starts at $169.99 for the ad-free version. With the price hikes, this is the Kindle that will remain the most affordable to new e-reader buyers.

The question I weighed was whether or not the basic Kindle is even worth buying at this price when there are arguably better Kindles on the market. The answer, after a couple of weeks of testing, is yes — if you can live without the bells and whistles and prefer a smaller, lighter device.

On the 6-inch Kindle, there’s no warm light to reduce eye strain, no color display, no auto-adjusting brightness, no option to use the page-turn cover, and it’s not waterproof. Obviously, because of its size, the screen is smaller, as is the battery. Battery life is 6 weeks compared with the Paperwhite’s 12 weeks or Colorsoft’s 8 weeks.

Still, even this basic Kindle has seen improvements of its own, mostly from a physical design perspective.

The plastic 2026 Kindle is 11% lighter and 14% thinner than the 2024 model, weighing 140g versus 158g and measuring 6.85mm thick versus 8mm. While this seems like a small change, the 18-gram difference is noticeable and particularly welcome for a device you’re likely to carry in your purse or bag. Plus, it makes it easier to hold for hours on end when you’re really binging your way through a book.

(The aluminum version, meanwhile, is slightly heavier at 162g, or 4 grams more than the 2024 Kindle, though it still benefits from the slimmer design.)

And despite being the “starter” Kindle, the 6-inch basic device still received the new flush-front screen update. This makes it more comfortable to hold in your hand, especially for those long reading sessions. Amazon explained that you don’t have to worry about no longer having a bezel to rest your thumb upon, either, as the new Kindles have been updated to detect a dead zone in the capacitive touch that will readjust to account for the fact that your finger is there.

In practice, that doesn’t mean you can just press your thumb down anywhere on the Kindle’s screen as you hold it — doing so would register this as an attempt to highlight or look up a word. Instead, it means you can rest your thumb or fingers on the outer edge of the Kindle’s screen (the colored border) without triggering an unintentional tap, even though some of your finger will be touching part of the Kindle’s capacitive screen.

In terms of the software, the new basic Kindle is a bit snappier than its 2024 predecessor. This is most noticeable when opening books, which Amazon claims to be 30% faster.

If you’re coming from the 2019 Kindle Basic, the 2026 version is an even bigger upgrade, as you gain USB-C, more storage (from 4GB to 8GB to now 16GB or 32GB), the new flush screen, and the screen resolution jumps from 167 ppi to 300 ppi. It’s faster, thinner, and lighter, too, and the battery lasts weeks longer.

Another perk about the basic Kindle beyond its small size (this thing fits in your jeans’ back pocket!), is that you can now pay a little more for an upgraded version with an aluminum backing instead of plastic and more storage. The new $189.99 aluminum option comes in Seagrass and Alpine Sky hues, and ships with 32GB of storage. Meanwhile, the $169.99 plastic model offers 16GB of storage.

However, even if you go for the less expensive option, you can at least now pick a fun color other than black (aka Graphite), as Amazon has introduced a cheery purple option called Ube. (I almost wish I’d gone for this one, just for the whimsy of it, even though I prefer the feel of the aluminum.)

I should point out that you can use the Kindle Click, the new Bluetooth remote for page turning, with the basic Kindle, but I’m not sure why you’d need to, if not for some accessibility-related reason. The 6-inch Kindle was already the smallest, and now it’s lighter and easier to hold, too. (But perhaps I just don’t get the appeal of the remote? I’ve barely used the remote with my Kobo either!)

The big thing to consider here is whether you want to spend this much on a Kindle that lacks a warm light. While this is something of a personal preference, for some readers, no warm light is a dealbreaker. The warm light shifts the color tone of the Kindle’s display from a cooler bluish-white to a softer amber glow, which is meant to help reduce eye strain and improve reading conditions in low light or at night.

Whether you need this feature depends on where you like to read and how long your sessions tend to be. If you read nightly in bed with little light, you might prefer paying extra for a $199.99 16GB Kindle Paperwhite. (That version only comes in Graphite. The 32GB Paperwhite can come in Seaglass, too, but is $249.99).

If you often read by the pool or on vacation, you also might want to upgrade to a waterproof Kindle.

But if you can live without the extra features and want the best purse- or pocket-sized device, the 6-inch Kindle is still a viable option.

#193. Armenia's selective prosecution: A threat to EU relations?

While Brussels has refrained from harsh criticism, Armenian civil society has warned of selective justice against opposition figures. Could the EU's pragmatic stance risk repeating past mistakes?

In early October, Artur Danielyan, leader of Armenia's opposition party Adekvad, was arrested following a Facebook post criticizing Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan.

The incident is part of a growing trend: Over the past two years, Armenian authorities have brought charges against multiple opposition figures, largely based on their social media activity.

Civil society representatives warn that such selective justice signals a worrying turn toward democratic backsliding.

The grounds for Danielyan's detention were Facebook posts in which he criticized both Pashinyan and the country's security services.

One point of contention was Pashinyan's stance on a possible prisoner exchange involving an Azerbaijani soldier accused of breaking into the home of a 39-year-old woman in the Armenian village of Shaki, and of injuring the woman and her children.

In an interview with Armenian news outlet Infocom, Pashinyan ruled out swapping the soldier imprisoned in Armenia for detained Armenians in Azerbaijan. Danielyan responded with a scathing attack, calling the prime minister a "scumbag" and accusing him of being unwilling to bring his fellow citizens home.

Armenia and Azerbaijan were in conflict for three decades over Nagorno-Karabakh, a breakaway Azerbaijani region populated by Armenians that declared independence in the 1990s. After Azerbaijan's military offensive in 2023, Baku regained control over the territory, forcing over 100,000 Armenians to flee. Currently, 19 Armenian individuals are being detained in Baku, including former high-ranking officials from Nagorno-Karabakh's de facto administration.

Over a dozen Armenian civil society organizations have condemned the prosecution of the Adekvad party leader, calling it "patently illegal, disproportionate, and politically motivated."

"It is punitive in nature and sends a direct signal to the broader public aimed at silencing dissent, critical views, and undesirable speech", said the joint statement.

Several other criminal proceedings have been launched against activists who criticized the ruling establishment or Pashinyan.

Another prominent case emerged ahead of the parliamentary election in June. Artur Osipyan, a displaced activist from Nagorno-Karabakh, was arrested after a verbal clash with Pashinyan over his Nagorno-Karabakh policy.

Following the incident, Armenian prosecutors indicted Osipyan for disrupting public order and obstructing the ruling party's campaign. He was also charged with inciting violence against Pashinyan in a social media post from March.

On April 15, 2020, Article 226.2 was added to Armenia's criminal code, penalizing public calls to violence, as well as the public justification or promotion of violence.

After strong outrage by civil society, these offenses were subsequently decriminalized. According to a 2025 report by Freedom House, "nearly 95 percent of court cases concerning incitement to violence under a 2020 criminal code amendment had involved alleged threats against Prime Minister Pashinyan and his supporters, whereas potentially prohibited statements by ruling party members were apparently not subject to the same scrutiny."

Throughout the 2026 pre-election period, the Regional Center for Democracy and Security, an independent think tank based in Yerevan, monitored online hate speech targeting Nagorno-Karabakh refugees.

Their reports documented how pro-government bloggers and influential social media users used their platforms to direct hostile rhetoric toward displaced Karabakh Armenians, labeling them with derogatory terms. Despite these findings, law enforcement agencies in Armenia largely refrained from pursuing criminal prosecutions against these activists.

Despite Armenia's efforts to strengthen its ties with the EU, Brussels has given no clear response to the silencing of opposition voices, observers in Yerevan told DW.

"The EU, by and large, has adopted a very pragmatic and geopolitically driven approach," said political analyst Tigran Grigoryan.

"Given various regional developments, including what is happening in Georgia, Armenia has now become the EU's primary partner in the region," he added. "Coupled with the fact that the alternative to Pashinyan is a pro-Russian opposition, there is ultimately no serious response to these criminal cases."

Stefan Meister, Eastern Europe expert at the German Council on Foreign Relations, echoed this view. European support for Armenia appears to be "mainly driven by the European Russia policy," Meister said. "So it's not so much about Armenia itself, but it is more about strengthening those forces that are undermining Russia's influence in the country and in the region."

Meister believes Pashinyan has leveraged this geopolitical dynamic to label internal political opponents as Russian proxies. However, not everyone who criticizes Pashinyan is pro-Russian, Meister added. He pointed out that "the EU is somehow falling into this trap by accepting that this is the right narrative."

Democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights are at the core of the EU-Armenia Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement and the Strategic Agenda for the EU-Armenia Partnership, an EU spokesperson said in a written response to DW's request for comment.

It also pointed out that "the EU is closely following developments in the country, including as regards criminal investigations. In line with Armenia's international commitments and legal framework, such investigations should be carried out in an independent and impartial manner, free from political considerations."

#191. Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

Editor’s Note:  A version of this story first appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in the Middle East newsletter, a three-times-a-week look inside the region’s biggest stories. Sign up here.

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet announced whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

“We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#189. Healthcare, tariffs – but not Trump impeachment: Democrats chart next two years of power

Midterms success gives party potent leverage over Trump – expect tough campaigns of investigating and lawmaking

“Costs, chaos, corruption”: after almost two years spent relentlessly criticizing Donald Trump for failing to address those three, broad political concerns, Democrats won a monumental return to power in Tuesday’s midterm elections that will give them potent new leverage over the president.

Now the question becomes: what will they do with it?

While party leaders say their exact strategy remains under discussion, all signs point to Democrats embarking on aggressive campaigns of both investigating and lawmaking, with the aim of giving their eventual nominee the ammunition they will need to win the 2028 presidential election.

“We are going to make sure that those candidates running for president of the United States aren’t getting asked about plastic-straw bans. Instead, we should be talking about all of the legislation that we pass out of the House, pass out of the Senate, and force to Donald Trump’s desk,” Greg Casar, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told reporters on Wednesday.

He envisioned “passing bold legislation that people called for, every single week, off of the floor of the House and the Senate”, pointing to bans on price gouging, Super Pacs and stock trading by lawmakers as priorities. “If [Trump] vetoes it, then that is the platform upon which candidates can run in 2028, and then we can get signed into law in 2029,” Casar said.

That election is still two, long and unpredictable years off. And despite flipping seats across the country, the Democratic party brand remains deeply unpopular.

But Democrats have reason to feel confident: Republicans suffered such a cataclysm Tuesday that they lost Senate seats they’d held for decades, and House seats drawn specifically to elect only Republicans.

It was the biggest midterm defeat for an incumbent party in more than 50 years, but the power Democrats have gained in Congress is not unlimited. Trump is still set to inhabit the White House until January 2029, and can veto bills that do not pass with overwhelming support.

And the Senate filibuster – which Democrats used to block many bills that Republicans attempted to pass along party lines over the first half of Trump’s second term – remains in place. Now the shoe is on the other foot: Republicans can use it to stop any incoming Democratic legislation that does not have 60 votes in a chamber. Ballot counting is still ongoing, but if the two outstanding Senate races are won by their candidates, Democrats and their allies will have 56 seats.

Congress’s incoming leaders have made clear those obstacles will not stop them from at least trying to enact legislative solutions to the problems they campaigned on fixing.

“We made a promise to the country that we would fight for an affordable America, and we intend to keep it,” said Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become speaker of the House of Representatives when the new Congress convenes after the new year.

He named as priorities reimplementing premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act (ACA) health plans as well as undoing the cuts to the Medicaid insurance program that Republicans approved last year. Jeffries also promised legislative action to make Trump undo his tariffs, and end the conflict with Iran.

“Everything we do maps onto three promises, the very same three we ran on, turning from a critique into a to-do list: lower costs, make your government work for you, clean up the corruption,” Chuck Schumer, who is expected to be the next Senate majority leader, said during an appearance at the Center for American Progress, a liberal thinktank.

One thing that does not seem to be on the table: impeaching Trump, for a third time. During his first term, Senate Republicans rescued the president after two impeachments, first on charges of leveraging aid to undermine his political rivals, and then again after his supporters attacked the Capitol on January 6.

While Democrats have accused Trump of violating the law and the constitution regularly during his second term, they appear clear-eyed about Republicans’ willingness to force the president from office.

“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” Jeffries said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability.”

When it comes to the latter, Democrats have no shortage of ideas. After publicly issuing a warning to potential targets to “lawyer up,” Robert Garcia, who will lead the investigative House oversight panel, told reporters this week to expect inquiries related to allegations of corruption in Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracting, stock trading by lawmakers, corporate profiteering and the government’s release of files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Noting he’d sent more than 200 demands for information to the Trump administration and others, Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House judiciary committee, said “go back and read my letters” when discussing who he would investigate next year. His letters carried no legal force, because he was in the congressional minority, but that will soon change – once the Democrats take committee gavels next year, they can issue subpoenas.

The party also doesn’t lack for ideas when it comes to addressing concerns about affordability, a major issue for voters in the elections.

It was Democrats’ demands to extend the ACA subsidies that led to the record-long government shutdown last year, and their candidates made warnings about the impending Medicaid cuts prominent in their campaigns.

The outgoing Republican congressional majorities have so far rejected attempts to address either issue, but Democrats did have some luck coaxing the majority to vote for war powers resolutions intended to end the conflict with Iran – one measure did pass, but the president has thus far ignored it.

“Trump has the ability to block our efforts to lower costs for American families, root out corruption in Washington, end the chaos in our streets and overseas,” Schumer acknowledged.

“But if he does that, I have no doubt the American people will rebuke him and his party just like they did in the election.”

So far, Trump, who cannot run again in 2028, has oscillated between saying he’d be willing to work with Democrats, and defiantly posting on social media an image of a red cap with the word “Veto” written on it.

The Democratic victories in the midterms came only after at-times anguished primaries that underscored the divides between the left and centers in the party, and over contentious issues like aid to Israel.

In the wake of their wins, leaders of the party’s ideological factions have taken tones of unity and cooperation – which could be aided by the fact that the Democratic majorities in both the Senate and House are expected to be so large that intraparty fights could be less impactful.

Kristen McDonald Rivet, who leads freshman lawmakers on the centrist New Democrat Coalition, acknowledged that when it comes to healthcare – a marquee issue for everyone in the party – “people want big change”.

“Some people’s approach to that is Medicare for all. Others are talking about Medicare for all who want it,” McDonald Rivet told reporters.

“There’s all kinds of ways to solve the solution, but I actually do not see that as a place of combat with other members of the caucus. It’s actually an incredibly hopeful thing that we are going to debate what big thing we can do around healthcare.”

#188. Parents want safer phones for kids. These companies are answering the call.

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

As parents become increasingly concerned about the potential dangers of unrestricted smartphone access for children, a growing number of companies are developing devices specifically designed for kids.

Today’s kid-friendly phones typically feature touchscreens, cameras, and communication capabilities similar to regular smartphones. However, the software on these devices is heavily modified to remove or restrict access to web browsers, social media, app stores, and other distractions.

Parents can usually manage these devices through a companion app, allowing them to approve contacts, monitor locations, set screen time limits, select available apps, and, in some cases, receive alerts regarding cyberbullying, explicit content, or online predators.

In addition to these modified devices, some companies offer a more minimalist approach, creating devices that focus solely on calling and texting.

There are also home phones designed specifically for children, like Tin Can and the recently launched Pinwheel Home.

Here’s a look at the major players shaping the kid-phone market.

The Bark Phone is probably one of the most popular kid-specific smartphones on the market.

Built on Samsung Galaxy hardware and powered by Bark’s monitoring software, it only allows calls and texts with approved contacts. Bark continuously scans texts, emails, photos, and supported apps for signs of cyberbullying, grooming, suicidal ideation, sexual content, and other potential concerns, then sends alerts to parents.

A big standout feature is that parents can gradually unlock web browsing, apps, and other features as their child matures. The phone also includes GPS tracking and screen-time management.

Current pricing for the standard model is $240, plus a required wireless plan beginning at $29/month. Higher-tier plans add internet access and unlimited texting.

Gabb is a well-known name in the kid-friendly phone category. Unlike Bark, however, Gabb focuses less on monitoring content and more on eliminating online risks altogether.

Its phones don’t include social media, a browser, or an app store. Instead, children get calling, texting, and a carefully curated selection of preloaded apps, including a camera, calendar, and calculator. The company also touts its “worry-free” music streaming library with millions of songs.

Additionally, parents can view location and manage certain device settings, while optional services such as “Gabb Guard” help block spam calls and unwanted texts.

Current phone pricing starts around $159.99, with cellular service starting around $24.99 per month.

With Pinwheel, parents approve every app, control contacts, schedule screen time, create custom routines, and monitor location history.

One standout feature is the ability to create different “modes” throughout the day. For example, limiting the phone to calling and navigation during school hours before unlocking additional features after homework.

Pinwheel phones start around $119, while the Caregiver Portal subscription begins at $14.99 per month without cell service. (Cellular service can be purchased separately through participating carriers.)

The company recently launched two landline phones for $68 and $79. It also offers a smartwatch at $160.

Launched in 2022, Teracube offers a tailored version of Android known as Thrive OS. This enables parents to approve every app download, filter web browsing, set app-specific and overall screen-time limits, monitor location, and create customized routines for school or bedtime. However, because it has more traditional smartphone features, it’s often recommended for older children.

Thrive currently sells for $99, with plans starting at $35 per month.

Unlike the other products in this roundup, Ooma MyPhone isn’t a mobile phone at all. This kid-focused home phone is designed as a modern replacement for the traditional household landline.

The service allows calls only between approved contacts through its Trusted Circle feature, offers scheduled Quiet Hours, provides address-based 911 service, sends emergency alerts when 911 is dialed, and lets parents review call logs through an online portal. There are no apps, internet browsing, texting, or social media.

The phone costs $99.99, while service starts at $7.99 per month.

For $100, Tin Can resembles a landline phone with a distinctive tin can design, which is the inspiration behind its name.

This device does not require a traditional phone jack, but connects via Wi-Fi. Only approved contacts can make calls, effectively preventing spam or unauthorized communications. Parents can easily manage contacts through a user-friendly companion app.

Tin Can offers a free plan for calling other Tin Can users, as well as a $9.99 per month plan that allows calls to all approved contacts.

A newer entrant in the space, Waffle recently opened preorders for its screen-free devices: Waffle Home ($119), a landline phone, and Waffle Go ($169), which looks like a portable walkie-talkie or kids’ toy with three simple buttons that can only make voice calls and listen to voice notes.

Parents can approve contacts via the companion app, as well as see location and control when devices can call.

TextNow, the Canadian telecommunications company, recently launched its new mobile phone for kids. It’s called Yello! and while it looks like a normal touchscreen smartphone, it doesn’t have an app store, social media, or unrestricted web access.

Parents can see their kids’ location and battery life, as well as control things like the games they play and who they have in their contacts.

Yello! costs $149.99 upfront, with a $19.99 per month plan.

Armed police attended the scene to search for the suspects. St Peter’s high school and the nearby Willow primary academy were put on lockdown on Friday after the attack.

A pupil named Jimmy at St Peter’s, a Catholic high school, told the BBC that the situation was “really scary” and students had been locked in their classrooms for several hours. “At the time I was scared,” he said. “My heart was racing.”

Parents also received messages from the school, explaining there had been an incident but that the situation was under control. #186. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.
